reason: The sources provide multi-site documentation of the Apollo light flash observations, ALFMED experiments, and underlying cosmic ray physics.
story: On the way to the Moon in 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts closed their eyes to rest in the dark cabin, only to see ghostly streaks and pinpoint flashes of light piercing their vision. Closing their eyelids offered no escape. Far beyond Earth's protective magnetic shield, high-energy cosmic rays were blasting through the spacecraft hull and slicing directly through the astronauts' eyeballs. When subatomic particles slammed into retinal photoreceptors or generated faint Cherenkov radiation inside the vitreous humor, the astronauts' brains perceived them as brilliant bursts of light. To investigate the phenomenon, NASA later had Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 astronauts strap on ALFMED, a helmet lined with radiation emulsions, proving that particle tracks coincided with the visual flashes. Later studies on space stations Mir and the ISS confirmed that even in complete darkness, deep space travelers were literally seeing cosmic radiation passing through their heads.
angle: Astronauts trying to sleep in deep space saw bright flashes of light with their eyes closed because high-energy cosmic rays were physically shooting through their eyeballs and hitting their retinas.

claims.claim: Apollo 11 astronauts observed mysterious flashes of light while resting in their spacecraft in 1969.
Buzz Aldrin documented seeing flashes of light while traveling toward the Moon on Apollo 11.
The light flashes were perceived even when astronauts closed their eyes or rested in dark environments.
Astronauts on Apollo flights 11 through 17 reported experiencing these visual light flashes.
The flashes manifested to astronauts in distinct shapes, including spots or dots, streaks or stripes, and clouds or blobs.
The visual phenomenon was determined to be caused by high-energy cosmic ray particles traversing the astronauts' eyes and visual systems.
One primary mechanism identified for the flashes is the direct interaction or ionization of cosmic ray particles with retinal photoreceptors.
Cherenkov radiation produced when charged particles travel through the eye's vitreous humor was investigated as a contributing mechanism.
During Apollo 16 and 17, astronauts tested the phenomenon using ALFMED, a helmet-like emulsion detector worn over the head.
The ALFMED experiment successfully correlated cosmic ray particle tracks with real-time flash observations reported by astronauts.
Apollo crews used light-tight eye shades during scheduled observation sessions to record flash characteristics.
On lunar missions, astronauts reported seeing light flashes more frequently during transit to the Moon than on the return trip to Earth.
Cosmic ray light flash phenomena have also been reported and studied by crews aboard the Mir space station.
The ALTEA project investigated cosmic ray light flashes and neural impacts aboard the International Space Station.

disputed: Whether Cherenkov radiation causes most flashes in space: Early hypotheses favored Cherenkov light in the vitreous humor, but later space and accelerator experiments suggested direct retinal ionization is the dominant cause; scripts should state that scientists consider multiple mechanisms, with direct retinal stimulation likely responsible for most flashes.

Flash frequency rates: S1 reports an average of once every 2.9 minutes for dark-adapted Apollo astronauts, while S4 gives an average of about once every two minutes; scripts should state 'roughly every two to three minutes'.
